openingProblem.problem:
Gorbachev introduced glasnost to save the Soviet system. He wanted open discussion to push a stubborn party into reform. Six years later the party had lost its monopoly of power, Lithuania had declared independence, and the leader who started it all had the support of about one Soviet citizen in five.

So was glasnost a tool that slipped out of his hands, or did it simply do what openness does to any one-party state?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: did glasnost destroy the system it was meant to save? Answer yes, no or partly, and give one reason.
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Has your judgement changed? Name the piece of evidence that changed it, or that confirmed it.

chunks.title: Why did Gorbachev turn to glasnost?
chunks.body:
Gorbachev became General Secretary on 11 March 1985. His first problem was not the economy itself but the party machine that ran it. The *apparat* resisted economic restructuring, and he could not purge it in the old way. Tony Judt argues that he therefore used glasnost as a lever: open discussion of a carefully limited range of topics would raise public expectations, and that public pressure would force reluctant officials to accept change. Glasnost began, in other words, as a method of control from above, not as a gift of freedom.

The word itself was not new. It already appeared in Article 9 of the 1977 Soviet constitution, and Gorbachev named glasnost and perestroika as key themes in a speech of December 1984, before he took power. What changed the slogan into a policy was the explosion at the Chernobyl nuclear plant on 26 April 1986. The leadership's first instinct was secrecy: Moscow's first acknowledgement came four days later, in a two-sentence communiqué. The cover-up failed because radiation crossed borders and the damage could not be contained. This mattered because it showed Gorbachev that secrecy itself was part of the system's failure, which meant that openness became a necessity rather than a tactic.

From late 1986 the change accelerated. Andrei Sakharov, the best-known dissident, was released from internal exile in Gorky in December 1986. In 1987 Vasily Grossman's long-delayed novel *Life and Fate* was published and the jamming of foreign radio stopped. In January 1987 Gorbachev used a televised speech to the Central Committee to argue for a more inclusive democracy, speaking over the heads of party conservatives. Because more than nine in ten Soviet households owned a television by 1987, this created a national audience for reform that the party could not ignore. In October 1987 he spoke publicly about Stalin's crimes for the first time.

The causal chain is therefore clear: a resistant apparatus led Gorbachev to seek outside pressure; Chernobyl discredited secrecy; and television turned his appeals into a public sphere. Each step widened glasnost beyond the narrow limits he first set.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Glasnost began as a tactic: Gorbachev needed public pressure to overcome the party apparatus.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The term was already in his December 1984 speech, so openness was part of his programme before any tactical need arose.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Chernobyl turned glasnost from a slogan into a policy.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The first response to Chernobyl was a cover-up, so the disaster shows the old reflex of secrecy as much as a new commitment to openness.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Releasing Sakharov and publishing banned works showed that openness was real, not only rhetorical.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: These were controlled concessions chosen by the leadership; they did not yet give citizens a right to criticise the party.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Glasnost began as a tactic to strengthen Gorbachev's hand against the party apparatus.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In January 1987 he used a televised Central Committee speech to argue for wider democracy, at a time when more than nine in ten households owned a television.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the debate moved out of the party's closed rooms and into a national audience, which put conservatives under public pressure.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the term was already in his December 1984 speech, so openness was also a goal in itself.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Glasnost was therefore largely instrumental at first, a means to economic reform rather than an end.

chunks.title: Democratisation: how far did power move away from the party?
chunks.body:
By 1988 Gorbachev had decided that openness alone could not beat the conservatives, so he changed the institutions. At the Nineteenth Party Conference in June 1988, the first such conference since 1941, he called for contested elections. In December 1988 the Supreme Soviet approved a new legislature, the Congress of People's Deputies, with 2,250 members. The design was cautious: one-third of the seats were reserved for the Communist Party and other official organisations, which was meant to guarantee a communist majority.

The March 1989 election was still the first time Soviet voters had chosen the members of a national legislature. Where only one official candidate stood, many voters crossed the name off the ballot, and prominent party officials were humiliated. The results show the two faces of democratisation: 87 per cent of the deputies were still party members, and genuine reformers won only about 300 seats, yet the old certainty that the party could not lose had gone.

What happened next mattered more than the arithmetic. When the Congress met in May 1989, its debates were shown live on television for two weeks; Judt estimates the audience at about 100 million. Deputies attacked the KGB, the military and Gorbachev himself. This broke the party's monopoly of information, because criticism now came from inside an official institution. In the summer of 1989 the first opposition bloc, the Interregional Group, formed; its co-chairs included Boris Yeltsin and Andrei Sakharov.

The last pillar to fall was Article 6 of the constitution, which gave the party its leading role. Under pressure from the opposition, and needing allies against hard-liners, Gorbachev secured the party's agreement to repeal it at the Central Committee plenum of February 1990. In March 1990 the Congress elected him to a new post of President of the USSR. He was chosen by the Congress, not by the voters, which left him with less democratic legitimacy than rivals who later won popular elections. Democratisation thus moved power out of the party, but it did not move it securely to Gorbachev.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Democratisation was real: for the first time Soviet voters chose a national legislature.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: One-third of the seats were reserved and 87 per cent of deputies were party members, so the outcome was managed from above.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Democratisation created rival centres of authority that Gorbachev could not control.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: A conservative majority still controlled the first Congress, so in 1989 the system was challenged rather than replaced.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Ending Article 6 removed the legal basis of one-party rule.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The change followed opposition pressure rather than leading it, so it registered the party's decline more than it caused it.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Democratisation weakened the party's control more than it strengthened Gorbachev's.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In the March 1989 elections voters crossed out unopposed officials, and when the Congress met in May its debates ran live on television for two weeks.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that criticism of the party now came from inside an official institution, so the party lost its monopoly of information as well as some of its seats.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, 87 per cent of the deputies were still party members, and a conservative majority controlled the Congress.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Democratisation was therefore only partly a transfer of power, but it decisively broke the party's monopoly of authority.

chunks.title: The nationalities question: why did openness turn into secession?
chunks.body:
In 1987 Gorbachev told the party that the nationalities issue had been resolved. Judt calls his belief that a little loosening would satisfy long-standing grievances a serious miscalculation. The Soviet state itself had created national republics, capitals and local elites, and when central control loosened, those elites were drawn to their own nations. Glasnost supplied the missing ingredient: permission to speak.

The first serious national conflict came in Alma-Ata in December 1986, when Gorbachev replaced the Kazakh party leader Dinmukhamed Kunaev with an ethnic Russian, Gennadii Kolbin. The protests were severely repressed. In February 1988 Armenians in the Karabakh enclave inside Azerbaijan demonstrated for union with Armenia, and the violence at Sumgait followed. In April 1988 activists in the Baltic republics began to form popular fronts, at first to defend language and culture.

The Baltic case shows the mechanism most clearly. Glasnost allowed people to discuss the 1939 Nazi–Soviet Pact, through which the three states had been absorbed into the USSR; the popular fronts demanded publication of its secret protocols. Because the history of annexation could now be discussed openly, cultural demands turned into political ones. On 9 July 1988 about 100,000 people rallied in Vilnius in support of Sajudis, the Lithuanian movement. In the March 1989 elections Sajudis won 36 of Lithuania's 42 seats, which meant that democratisation handed the national movement a democratic mandate. On 23 August 1989, the fiftieth anniversary of the pact, an estimated 1.8 million people formed a human chain of about 650 kilometres from Vilnius to Tallinn.

Moscow's responses swung between force and retreat, which weakened it either way. Soldiers shot twenty demonstrators in Tbilisi in April 1989. When Lithuania's Supreme Soviet voted 124–0 to restore independence on 11 March 1990, Moscow answered with an economic boycott and then dropped it. In January 1991 troops killed fourteen civilians in Vilnius. Yet nationalism was not irresistible everywhere: in the referendum of 17 March 1991, 76.4 per cent of those who voted backed a renewed Union, although six republics refused to take part.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Glasnost turned national grievances into organised movements by allowing open discussion of history.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The republics, their capitals and their local elites were Soviet creations that predated glasnost, so the structure of the state made national politics likely anyway.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Democratisation gave national movements a democratic mandate that Moscow could not easily dismiss.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The March 1991 referendum showed most participating voters still wanted a renewed Union, so secession was strongest in particular republics, not universal.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Gorbachev misjudged the national question and then used force inconsistently, losing both nationalists and hard-liners.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: His refusal to use force systematically also kept violence far lower than a full crackdown would have caused.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Glasnost was the decisive cause of Baltic nationalism because it made the history of annexation discussable.
useItInAnEssay.prove: On 23 August 1989, the fiftieth anniversary of the Nazi–Soviet Pact, an estimated 1.8 million people formed a human chain from Vilnius to Tallinn.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that a protest about the past became a mass claim to independence, organised by popular fronts that glasnost had allowed to exist.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the republics and their national elites were created by the Soviet state itself, so the structure of the Union made national politics likely.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Glasnost therefore did not create Baltic nationalism, but it largely explains why it became a mass movement by 1989.

chunks.title: Did Gorbachev lose control, or let go?
chunks.body:
Abroad, Gorbachev let go on purpose. In his speech to the United Nations on 7 December 1988 he announced unilateral cuts in Soviet conventional forces and declared that freedom of choice was a universal principle with no exceptions. Judt reads this as more than a renunciation of the Brezhnev Doctrine: the satellite states were now free to choose their own path. The US Library of Congress study is more cautious, noting that a July 1989 speech to the Council of Europe on each people's right to choose its own social system fell just short of repudiating the doctrine. Either way, the signal mattered, because it removed the threat of Soviet force behind the Brezhnev Doctrine, which had kept communist governments in power in the bloc. This is the causal link to the collapse of Soviet control in central and eastern Europe in 1989.

At home the picture is of control slipping away. Party hard-liners hated the reforms: in a letter published in *Sovetskaya Rossiya* on 13 March 1988, the Leningrad teacher Nina Andreyeva warned that they would lead back to capitalism. Radical reformers such as Yakovlev and Yeltsin, meanwhile, thought he moved too slowly. Gorbachev tried to hold the centre ground, encouraging new ideas and then retreating towards the conservatives. Judt argues that by giving up the party's monopoly he also gave up his own main source of power, so he had to bargain like a democratic politician in a country used to dictatorship. The result was that he looked weak to both sides: by the autumn of 1990 only 21 per cent of the public supported him.

The decision to be elected President by the Congress rather than by the people sharpened the problem. When Yeltsin won a popular election as President of the Russian republic in June 1991, many saw him as more legitimate than Gorbachev. The leader who had opened the system now had no independent base inside it.

The judgement turns on intention. Abroad, Gorbachev chose not to use force and accepted the consequences. At home he wanted a reformed, united, socialist Union and did not intend its break-up, so there the outcome was a loss of control rather than a decision to let go.

argumentsThatWork.claim: In foreign policy Gorbachev deliberately gave up the threat of force.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Library of Congress study notes that his 1989 formulation fell just short of repudiating the Brezhnev Doctrine, and at home he still used force in Vilnius in January 1991.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Holding the centre ground made Gorbachev look weak to conservatives and radicals alike.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Once the party's monopoly had gone, any leader would have struggled to hold the centre; the problem was structural, not only personal.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Choosing indirect election left Gorbachev without a popular mandate.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: A popular election in 1990 carried the risk of defeat, so the indirect route was a rational choice at the time.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Gorbachev deliberately ended the threat of Soviet force in eastern Europe.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In his speech to the United Nations on 7 December 1988 he announced unilateral troop cuts and called freedom of choice a universal principle.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the governments of the bloc could no longer rely on Soviet tanks, which removed the guarantee behind communist rule in the satellite states.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the Library of Congress study notes that his July 1989 statement still fell just short of repudiating the Brezhnev Doctrine.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Gorbachev's role was therefore decisive abroad, where he chose to let go, but at home he lost control rather than chose to give it up.

historiography.argument: Glasnost began as a tactic: open discussion of a restricted range of topics, used to pry loose the party apparatus's opposition to reform, and Gorbachev's belief that loosening control would satisfy the nationalities was a serious miscalculation.
historiography.useItLikeThis: Judt's view that glasnost was a lever against the apparatus supports the claim that its destructive effects were unintended, which suggests the collapse of party authority was a loss of control rather than a plan.

historiography.argument: Glasnost was a “facilitating concept” that writers and journalists pushed beyond the limits Gorbachev intended, so in practice it became a right asserted from below.
historiography.useItLikeThis: Brown's argument challenges a purely top-down reading, which suggests that glasnost's impact depended as much on society's response as on Gorbachev's aims.

misconceptions.wrong: Glasnost meant full freedom of speech from 1985.
misconceptions.right: It began as official encouragement to discuss a **restricted** range of topics and widened from late 1986, partly because society pushed beyond the limits.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was glasnost responsible for the collapse of Communist Party authority in the Soviet Union between 1985 and 1991?
essayQuestions.scope: Soviet Union; authority of the Communist Party

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far, using degree language
decodeKey.scope: The party's authority in the Soviet Union
decodeKey.judgement: How far glasnost, compared with democratisation, nationalism and Gorbachev's choices, caused the collapse

modelPlan.thesis: Glasnost was largely responsible because it broke the party's monopoly of information, but it became decisive only in combination with democratisation, which turned public criticism into organised, elected opposition.

arguments.claim: Glasnost broke the party's monopoly of information (named factor first).
Democratisation turned criticism into institutions: the Congress, the Interregional Group and the end of Article 6.
National movements removed the party's authority in the republics.
Gorbachev's centrism cost him support on both sides.

modelPlan.counter: Glasnost only exposed failures that already existed: secrecy had failed at Chernobyl, and the national republics were Soviet creations.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which factor, if removed, would most have slowed the collapse? Without glasnost the other factors lose their voice, so it is the necessary condition, but democratisation was the sufficient one.

segments.text: Glasnost was largely responsible for the collapse of party authority because it ended the party's monopoly of information.
When the Congress of People's Deputies met in May 1989, its debates ran live on television for two weeks, to an audience Judt estimates at about 100 million.
This meant that attacks on the KGB, the military and Gorbachev came from inside an official institution, so the party could no longer present criticism as the work of isolated dissidents.
However, the broadcasts mattered only because democratisation had created the Congress; glasnost alone, in 1986–87, had produced debate but not opposition.
Glasnost was therefore the necessary condition of the collapse of party authority, but not on its own a sufficient one.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Gorbachev's democratisation weakened rather than strengthened the Soviet state between 1987 and 1990.” Discuss.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: consider the case for and against the proposition, then reach a balanced conclusion
decodeKey.factorOrTask: Democratisation and whether it weakened or strengthened the state
decodeKey.scope: The Soviet state as a whole, not only the party
decodeKey.judgement: On balance, did democratisation weaken the state more than it strengthened it?

modelPlan.thesis: Democratisation strengthened the state's legitimacy in the short term, but on balance it weakened the state, because the institutions it created became platforms for opposition that the centre could not control.

arguments.claim: For the proposition: democratisation created rival centres of authority (named factor first).
For the proposition: elections gave national movements a mandate.
Against: the first contested elections gave Soviet institutions a new legitimacy and drew reformers into the system.
Against: the design kept a communist majority, so in 1989 the state was challenged rather than broken.

modelPlan.counter: The state was already weakened by economic failure and by the national structure of the Union; democratisation exposed this rather than causing it.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Judge by the state's ability to enforce its decisions: by 1990 it could not stop Lithuania's declaration, which shows weakness.

segments.text: Democratisation weakened the Soviet state because the institutions it created soon became platforms for opposition.
In the summer of 1989 the Interregional Group formed inside the new Congress, with Yeltsin and Sakharov among its co-chairs, and in February 1990 the Central Committee agreed to repeal Article 6.
This meant that the state's legal centre, the party, lost its leading role at the moment when organised critics had gained a national stage.
On the other hand, the first contested elections in March 1989 gave Soviet institutions a legitimacy they had never had, which in the short term strengthened the state.
On balance, democratisation weakened the state more than it strengthened it, because the new legitimacy flowed to its critics rather than to the centre.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the reasons for, and the consequences of, the growth of national movements in the Soviet Union between 1985 and 1991.
essayQuestions.scope: National movements in the Soviet republics

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh the relative importance of reasons and the significance of consequences, with a criterion
decodeKey.factorOrTask: Two parts: reasons for growth; consequences
decodeKey.scope: The Soviet republics (Baltic, Caucasus, Central Asia)
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The growth of national movements was caused above all by glasnost's permission to discuss the past, made potent by democratisation, and its most significant consequence was that the Union's authority collapsed in the republics before it collapsed in Moscow.

arguments.claim: Reason: glasnost allowed open discussion of grievances and history.
Reason: democratisation gave national movements mandates.
Consequence: declarations of independence that Moscow could not reverse.
Consequence: the March 1991 referendum exposed a divided Union.

modelPlan.counter: Some movements were triggered by Moscow's own clumsiness, such as Kolbin's appointment in 1986, rather than by glasnost.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Judge reasons by whether the movement could have grown without them; judge consequences by their effect on the Union's survival.

segments.text: The most important reason for the growth of national movements was glasnost, because it made the history of annexation discussable.
On 23 August 1989, the fiftieth anniversary of the Nazi–Soviet Pact, an estimated 1.8 million people formed a human chain from Vilnius to Tallinn.
This meant that cultural grievances became a claim to independence, organised by popular fronts that could only exist under glasnost.
However, the Alma-Ata protests of December 1986 were triggered by Moscow's appointment of Kolbin, which shows that clumsy central decisions also caused national protest.
Glasnost was therefore the more significant reason, because it turned scattered protest into lasting movements.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the aims and results of glasnost and democratisation in the Soviet Union between 1985 and 1991.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, point by point
decodeKey.factorOrTask: Aims and results of two policies
decodeKey.judgement: Were the two policies more alike or more different in aims and results?

modelPlan.thesis: Both policies aimed to force the party to reform from outside its apparatus, but they differed in method and result: glasnost changed what could be said, whereas democratisation changed who held power, and so it did more damage to the party.

arguments.claim: Similar aims: both were tools to overcome the apparatus.
Similar results: both escaped Gorbachev's limits.
Different methods: glasnost relied on discussion and media, democratisation on elections and institutions.
Different results: democratisation ended the leading role of the party.

modelPlan.counter: The two cannot be fully separated: the televised Congress was both glasnost and democratisation.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Judge by impact on the party's power: democratisation's result was more radical than glasnost's.

segments.text: Both glasnost and democratisation aimed to push the party into reform from outside its apparatus.

Glasnost worked through public discussion, such as the televised Central Committee speech of January 1987, whereas democratisation worked through elections, beginning with the contested elections of March 1989.
This difference in method meant that glasnost changed what could be said, while democratisation changed who held office, so the second struck directly at the party's power.
However, the two overlapped: the televised first session of the Congress in May 1989 was the product of both policies.
The policies were therefore similar in aim but different in result, and democratisation did more to end the party's monopoly.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the role of Gorbachev in the rise of nationalist movements in the Baltic republics between 1987 and 1991.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: consider the evidence and the assumptions behind Gorbachev's role
decodeKey.judgement: How central was Gorbachev's role, compared with long-standing national grievances?

modelPlan.thesis: Gorbachev's role was central but unintended: his reforms gave Baltic movements the freedom and the mandate to organise, while his inconsistent use of force strengthened rather than stopped them.

arguments.claim: Gorbachev's glasnost allowed open discussion of the Nazi–Soviet Pact (named factor first).
His democratisation gave Sajudis an electoral mandate.
His responses to the 1990 declaration and the 1991 violence weakened Moscow's position.

modelPlan.counter: Baltic grievances about annexation long predated Gorbachev; he released them rather than created them.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Judge by timing: the movements became mass movements only after his reforms.

segments.text: Gorbachev's role in the rise of Baltic nationalism was central, because his democratisation turned protest into a democratic mandate.
In the March 1989 elections Sajudis won 36 of Lithuania's 42 seats.
This meant that Lithuanian demands now came from elected deputies, which made them much harder for Moscow to dismiss as the work of agitators.
However, the grievance itself, the annexation that followed the 1939 Nazi–Soviet Pact, long predated Gorbachev.
Gorbachev's role was therefore decisive in the timing and strength of Baltic nationalism, though not in its origins.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the impact of the Chernobyl disaster on Soviet policy towards openness between 1986 and 1989.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the impact into parts and explain the links
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The Chernobyl disaster and its impact
decodeKey.judgement: How far, and how, Chernobyl changed policy

modelPlan.thesis: Chernobyl changed glasnost from a slogan into a policy, because the failed cover-up showed that secrecy itself endangered the state, but the disaster accelerated a commitment that already existed rather than creating it.

arguments.claim: The failed cover-up discredited secrecy (named factor first).
After Chernobyl the media began investigative reporting and openness widened.
Openness spread from environmental issues to politics and history.

modelPlan.counter: Gorbachev had named glasnost as a key theme in December 1984, so the policy predated the disaster.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Judge by change over time: before April 1986 glasnost was little more than a slogan; after it, it shaped policy.

segments.text: The Chernobyl disaster turned glasnost from a slogan into a policy.
After the explosion on 26 April 1986, Moscow's first acknowledgement came only four days later, in a two-sentence communiqué.
This meant that the leadership saw secrecy fail in public, because radiation crossed borders and could not be hidden, which made openness a necessity rather than a choice.
However, Gorbachev had already named glasnost as a key theme in December 1984, so the disaster accelerated a commitment rather than creating it.
Chernobyl's impact on policy towards openness was therefore decisive in timing and urgency, though not in origin.
